consensus_summary: All three blind responses converge on Egypt as a symbol of bondage/slavery to sin and the oppressive world-system out of which God redeems his people, grounded in the Exodus paradigm ('house of bondage'), with secondary strands of false security/misplaced trust, imperial pride under judgment, refuge/providential shelter, and (in one response) a note that some apply Revelation 11:8's 'Sodom and Egypt' to unfaithful Jerusalem.
book_summary: The book identifies 'Egypt' spiritually as a specific city: Jerusalem — the whore of Babylon riding the beast, the city that kills the prophets and 'where also our Lord was crucified' (Rev 11:8). It explicitly notes and sets aside the commonly taught meaning (bondage to sin and the world-system).
consensus_core_identification: Egypt = bondage/slavery to sin and the godless world-system from which God delivers his people (Exodus as paradigm of redemption).
book_core_identification: Egypt = Jerusalem, spiritually named — the prophet-killing city where the Lord was crucified, further identified with the whore of Babylon.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus treats Egypt as an abstract condition/system (bondage, worldliness) applicable typologically to any believer's old life; the book fixes the symbol to a single concrete referent, apostate Jerusalem. Only Response A's second alternative brushes against this ('some interpreters apply this specifically to unfaithful Jerusalem'), but even there Egypt is an emblem of the God-opposing world order generally, not an identification of Egypt with Jerusalem as the symbol's meaning.
material_contradiction: The consensus says Egypt symbolizes the world of sin/bondage out of which God's people are called; the book says the spiritual meaning of Egypt is Jerusalem itself (and equates it with Babylon's whore). One cannot hold that Egypt's spiritual referent is the generic world-system of bondage and simultaneously that it is specifically the covenant city Jerusalem; the book expressly flags and displaces the common teaching in its own note.
rationale: The book's own 'commonly taught' note matches the blind consensus, confirming the baseline. Its actual entry replaces that abstract identification with a concrete referent: Jerusalem, via a chain running Rev 11:8 (great city spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where the Lord was crucified) → Matt 23:37 (Jerusalem kills the prophets) → Gal 4:25 (Jerusalem in bondage) → Isa 1:10 (Jerusalem's rulers addressed as Sodom) → Rev 18:24 (Babylon holds the prophets' blood). This is not a narrowing of the consensus's category (bondage/world-system) but a substitution of the central referent, so it is DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the Jerusalem application of Rev 11:8 is glancingly acknowledged in Response A as an interpreter's option, but as a minority gloss on one verse, not as the symbol's core meaning — the book's wholesale identification (including the Babylon-whore equation) contradicts rather than merely refines the consensus core.
strongest_objection: Response A explicitly notes that 'some interpreters apply this specifically to unfaithful Jerusalem' under Revelation 11:8, so one could argue the book's reading is already a listed alternative and the relation is REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. However, that alternative frames Egypt as an emblem of the God-opposing world order with Jerusalem as one application; the book instead makes Jerusalem the definitional spiritual referent of Egypt itself and fuses it with the whore of Babylon, which replaces rather than qualifies the consensus identification.
